FOR DENTAL PRACTICE OWNERS AND OFFICE MANAGERS

Your fee schedule is not what you collect.

Every practice knows its total write-off. Almost none knows it per plan — and per plan is the only form in which two contracts can be compared. The adjustment is posted the moment the claim is, in a column no report turns into a rate, so the contract taking the most out of the practice is rarely the one that feels worst. Put one month in below and see what each carrier actually pays, which of them buy chair time for less than the chair costs, and what a fee increase would really collect.

      Common questions

      How do I work out my effective reimbursement rate for each PPO plan?

      Divide what a carrier actually paid by what you billed it at your own fee schedule — net production over gross production, per plan. That is the whole calculation, and it is the only form in which two contracts can be compared, because a dollar adjustment says nothing about the fee it was taken from. Put one month in above and the tool does the division for every carrier at once, then ranks them.

      Where do I find the write-off figure for each carrier?

      A production-by-carrier report for one month gives you both columns this page needs: production posted at your own fee schedule, and the contractual adjustment written off against it. Your practice management system may call that adjustment a write-off, a contractual, or a PPO adjustment; it is the line posted at the moment the claim is, not a bad debt anyone chased. Only period totals per carrier are entered here — no procedure-level or patient-level figures are used.

      Will raising my fee schedule reduce my write-offs?

      On contracted production, no — and this is the result most practices are surprised by. An allowed fee is a contracted dollar amount, not a percentage of whatever you happen to charge, so raising your UCR fees raises gross production and the write-off by exactly the same amount and collects nothing extra. A fee rise moves money only on production that is not contracted, which for most practices means self-pay. Enter a percentage above and the tool shows all three figures separately: added production billed, added write-off, and added collections.

      If a plan pays below my break-even rate, should I drop it?

      This tool does not answer that, and you should not read a red bar as saying so. The break-even rate is your cost per chair hour divided by your gross production per chair hour, so a plan below it is buying chair time for less than the chair costs to keep open — on the month you entered, under the hour allocation described below. What it does not model is what would happen to those hours afterwards: dropped contract hours do not automatically refill with better-paying work, and network participation carries patient-retention, referral and contractual consequences that are nowhere in this arithmetic. Treat the ranking as a place to start a conversation with your own advisers.

      Why does it allocate chair hours by production instead of asking for hours per carrier?

      Because almost no practice tracks chair time by carrier, so a tool that demanded it could not be filled in from any report that already exists. Your own fee schedule is, by construction, your own pricing of chair time: an hour billed at $600 of UCR is an hour of chair whatever a carrier later allows. So hours are allocated between plans in proportion to gross production at your fees. That makes it an assumption written down where you can check it rather than a guess hidden inside the result.

      Does any of this leave my computer?

      No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser, there is no account, nothing is uploaded, and there is deliberately no shareable link — a practice's production, payroll and overhead should not ride in a URL. Saving a month writes the figures to this browser's own storage and clearing your browser data clears them. No patient-level information is an input to begin with, so nothing you type here is protected health information.

      What this is, and is not

      No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, employment or contract advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, which networks to join or leave, how to code or record any adjustment, or how any agreement should be read. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every figure against your own practice management system, payroll records and accounts, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or acting on a contract with it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

vs-ppo-fee-negotiators.html.text:
← Dental PPO Write-Off Calculator

This calculator vs. hiring a PPO fee negotiator

Different jobs. A fee-schedule negotiation service renegotiates a contracted rate with a carrier, usually for a flat fee per payer or a cut of the increase. This free calculator does not negotiate anything — it tells you, from your own numbers, which contract is worth paying someone to negotiate.

What each one is for

A PPO fee-schedule negotiation service does the part this calculator cannot: it contacts a carrier and actually negotiates a higher contracted allowed fee. These services generally charge one of two ways — a flat fee per payer contract, or a percentage of the reimbursement increase they secure, sometimes continuing as a share of the higher collections going forward. That is real, billable work, and if a contract is worth renegotiating, a service that does this full time is better placed to do it than a practice owner between patients.

This calculator does the part that comes before paying anyone. It takes one month of production and contractual write-offs, split by carrier — a report every practice management system already produces — and ranks every plan by the dollars its write-off takes, with the effective reimbursement rate printed alongside. Those are frequently not the same plan: a low-volume plan can carry the worst rate in the practice and still cost the least in dollars, while a middling-rate, high-volume plan quietly takes the most. Paying a flat per-payer fee, or a cut of the increase, on the wrong contract is money spent on the plan that looked worst rather than the one that actually mattered.

It also answers a question worth settling before any negotiation begins: whether raising your own posted fee schedule would collect anything at all. A PPO's allowed fee is a contracted dollar amount, not a percentage of whatever the practice charges, so raising your own fee schedule on already-contracted procedures raises the write-off by the same amount it raises gross production and collects nothing. Only a changed contracted rate — the thing a negotiator is hired to get — touches money a PPO agreement has already locked in. This calculator prints both figures side by side so that difference is visible before a fee schedule change or a negotiation engagement is chosen.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Which of my contracts is actually costing the most, in dollars?This calculator's per-plan ranking — free, private, no account, and different from ranking by rate alone.
Would raising my own fee schedule collect more from my PPO plans?This calculator's fee-increase model — on contracted procedures, usually close to nothing.
Can I actually get a carrier to pay a higher contracted rate?A PPO fee-schedule negotiation service. This calculator cannot contact a carrier or negotiate anything.
Is a per-payer fee or a percentage-of-increase engagement worth it for a given plan?Start with this calculator's ranking, then take the plan(s) with the largest dollar write-off to a negotiator.
What is my break-even reimbursement rate, so I can tell if a plan pays less than the chair costs?This calculator — from your own cost and production per chair hour.
Do I need an account or a sign-in?This calculator: no. A negotiation service is a paid engagement with a signed agreement.

The two are sequential, not competing: this calculator to find and size the problem for free, a negotiation service to actually fix the contract if the dollars justify the fee. This page is arithmetic on numbers you provide, not a negotiation, a guarantee of any carrier response, or advice about which service to hire.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or hire a PPO fee-schedule negotiation service?

Both, in that order. A fee-schedule negotiation service does something this calculator cannot: it contacts carriers and actually renegotiates a contracted rate, usually charging a flat fee per payer or a percentage of the increase it wins. This calculator does not negotiate anything and cannot promise any carrier will move. What it does first, for free, from one month of your own production and adjustment numbers, is tell you which of your contracts is actually costing the most in dollars — not which has the worst rate, which is often a different plan — so that a flat per-payer fee or a percentage cut goes toward the contract that is genuinely worth pursuing rather than the one that merely looks worst on paper.

How do PPO fee-schedule negotiation services usually charge?

Typically one of two ways: a flat fee per payer contract, or a percentage of the reimbursement increase the service secures, sometimes billed as an ongoing share of the higher collections. Either way you are paying for the negotiation itself, not for knowing which contract to negotiate first — and concentrating that spend on the plan with the largest write-off in dollars is what this calculator's ranking is for.

If I raise my own fee schedule, is that the same as negotiating a better contracted rate?

No, and conflating the two is the single most common reason a practice thinks it fixed a write-off and did not. A PPO's allowed fee is a contracted dollar amount, not a percentage of whatever the practice charges. Raising your own posted fee schedule on a procedure that is already contracted raises the gross production figure and the write-off by exactly the same amount, and collects nothing. It only moves money on production that is not covered by a plan. A negotiator changes the contracted allowed fee itself, which is the only lever that touches money already locked in by a PPO agreement. This calculator prints both figures side by side so the difference is visible before either is attempted.

Does this calculator negotiate with insurance carriers?

No. It is arithmetic on numbers you already have — one month of production and contractual adjustments, per plan, from a report your practice management system already produces. It has no contact with any carrier and cannot promise any contract will change. That work, if you want it done, is what a fee-schedule negotiation service is hired to do.

Is a bad reimbursement rate the same problem as a big write-off?

Often not, which is exactly where a flat per-payer negotiation fee can be spent on the wrong contract. A low-volume plan can carry a terrible rate and still take a small number of dollars out of the practice each month, while a high-volume plan with a middling rate can be the one actually costing the most. This calculator ranks every plan by write-off dollars, with its rate printed alongside, so the two questions — which rate is worst, and which contract is worth paying to fix — are answered separately rather than assumed to be the same plan.

Open the Dental PPO Write-Off Calculator to run your own numbers.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, employment, or contract advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. It does not negotiate with, contact, or represent you to any carrier, and it cannot predict or guarantee the outcome of any negotiation. Verify every figure against your own practice management system before relying on it or acting on a contract with it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. This page describes PPO fee-schedule negotiation services in general terms; it does not name, endorse, or compare against any specific negotiation company.

Free and open source. If it helps you decide where to spend a negotiation budget, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-practice-management-report.html.text:
← Dental PPO write-off calculator

This calculator vs. your practice management system's reports

Your practice management system already holds every number on this page. It reports production and it reports contractual adjustments, both as dollar columns, usually organised by provider, by procedure, or by day. What it does not do is divide one by the other per carrier — because that division only means something once you fix a period and a contract, which is not how the reports are grouped.

So the figure a practice ends up holding is a practice-wide write-off total: real money, correctly reported, and impossible to act on, because it names no contract. The contractual adjustment is posted at the same moment as the claim, never ages, is chased by nobody, and appears in no collections report. It is the only money a practice loses that never looks like a loss. This calculator takes three figures per plan off a report you already run and turns them into a rate the contracts can be compared on.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What did we produce and what did we write off last quarter? Your practice management system. It is the system of record and this page cannot replace it.
Which claims are outstanding, and what is on tomorrow's schedule? Your practice management system. This page holds no ledger, no claims and no patient data.
What rate is each carrier actually reimbursing us at? This calculator's effective reimbursement rate, per plan and blended — net over gross at your own fee schedule.
Which contract is costing us the most — not which has the worst rate? This calculator's plan table, ranked by write-off dollars with the rate printed beside it. The worst rate is routinely not the biggest number.
Is any plan buying chair time for less than the chair costs to keep open? This calculator's break-even reimbursement rate, stated as a rate so it lines up against the per-plan rates by eye.
Is our write-off one bad contract or eight mediocre ones? This calculator's concentration reading — how many carriers make up half of it. The same total, two entirely different problems.
If we raise the fee schedule, what would we actually collect? This calculator's fee-increase model, which separates what an increase collects from what it merely adds to the write-off.
Work out your own rates

No account, upload, or subscription: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your figures stay on your device. Every input is a period total for a carrier — production, write-off, chair hours, payroll, overhead — so no protected health information is involved at any point. Saving a scenario writes to this browser's own storage only.

Common questions

Which report do I run to fill this in?

Whatever your system calls a production-by-carrier or insurance-analysis report, for one closed period. You need three figures per plan: gross production at your own fee schedule, the contractual adjustment written off, and the period the two cover. Practice-wide you need chair hours worked, payroll and provider compensation, and practice overhead. Every one of those is a period total, not a patient record, so nothing protected leaves your system and nothing needs to be exported anywhere.

Can my practice management system work out the effective rate itself?

Some systems can be made to, with a custom report or a query, and if yours already prints a reimbursement rate per carrier then you do not need this page for that number. What no stock report does is rank the plans by the write-off dollars they take, state a break-even rate to compare them against, or separate what a fee schedule increase would collect from what it would merely add to the write-off. Those are the three outputs this calculator exists for.

Should I use this instead of my management system?

No, and it could not replace one. Your management system is the system of record: it holds the ledger, the claims, the schedule and the patient data, and every figure typed here comes out of it. This is a single-screen piece of arithmetic you run on top of a report you already have, for a question the report is not organised to answer. Check its output back against your own numbers before acting on it.

Why does the report name no carrier and this page ask me to?

Because the division only means something once you fix a period and a carrier. A practice-wide adjustment total names no contract, so it cannot be acted on: there is no decision whose answer changes when the total moves. A rate per carrier is the form in which two contracts can be compared, and comparing them is the only reason to compute it. The carrier labels stay in your browser and are never uploaded.

Is this page affiliated with any practice management system?

No. This page names no specific practice management system, makes no claim about any particular vendor's reports or features, and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any of them. It describes practice management systems as a category, because every practice has one and the reports they produce are organised the same way for this purpose.

What is my effective reimbursement rate? works through the arithmetic itself, with a worked example.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, employment or contract advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, which networks to join or leave, how to code or record any adjustment, or how any agreement should be read. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every figure against your own practice management system, payroll records and accounts, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or acting on a contract with it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

what-is-my-effective-reimbursement-rate..text:
DENTAL PRACTICE ECONOMICS

What is my effective reimbursement rate, and why is it lower than I think?

It is one division: net production over gross production, for one carrier, over one period. If you billed $62,000 at your own fee schedule last month under a single PPO and $24,800 came off as a contractual adjustment, that plan reimbursed you at 60%. Everything else on this page follows from that number being computed per plan rather than in total.

Open the free calculator

Why no report shows it

A practice management system reports production, and it reports adjustments, and both are dollar columns. Nothing divides one by the other, because the division only means something once you fix a period and a carrier — and the report is organised by provider, by procedure, or by day. So the practice ends up knowing one figure, the total write-off, which is the one figure that cannot be acted on: it names no contract.

The adjustment is also posted at the same moment as the claim. It never ages, nobody chases it, and it appears in no collections report. It is the only money a practice loses that never looks like a loss.

The plan with the worst rate is usually not the plan costing you most

Rate and dollars rank differently, and a practice reading only one of them will work on the wrong contract. A plan reimbursing 55% on $31,000 of production takes $13,950. A plan reimbursing 60% on $62,000 takes $24,800. The second has the better rate and costs nearly twice as much.

Delta PPO — 60% of $62,000
$24,800
Cigna — 55% of $31,000
$13,950
Delta Premier — 80% of $48,000
$9,600
MetLife — 65% of $19,000
$6,650

An illustration, not a benchmark. These are the figures the calculator opens on so you can see the shape before entering your own; they are not a survey of what carriers pay and nothing should be inferred about any named plan from them.

The number that decides whether a contract is worth having

Work out what an hour of chair costs: provider compensation plus practice overhead, over clinical chair hours. Then work out what you produce in that hour at your own fees. The ratio of the two is a break-even reimbursement rate — and because it is a rate, it sits directly alongside the per-plan rates and the comparison takes no arithmetic at all.

A practice costing $176.56 an hour to run and producing $312.50 an hour at its own fees breaks even at 56.5%. Every plan above that rate contributes something to the practice; every plan below it is selling chair time for less than the chair costs to keep open.

That is a fact about the contract, not a recommendation about it. Terminating an agreement removes the write-off and the production together, and whether the practice is better off depends entirely on how much of that schedule refills at your own fees — a question about your market and your patients that no calculator can answer.

Why raising your fee schedule collects almost nothing

This is the one most practices get wrong, and it is worth being exact about. A PPO allowed fee is a contracted dollar amount. It does not move when your posted fee moves. So on every contracted procedure, raising your fee raises the gross production you bill and raises the write-off by precisely the same amount. The collection is unchanged.

A fee increase collects more only on production that is not contracted. In a practice where 80% of production runs through plans, an 8% rise across the schedule bills $16,000 more, writes off $12,800 of it, and collects $3,200. The write-off percentage — the figure that gets watched — gets worse, while the practice is slightly better off. Both halves of that are worth knowing before the decision, and the calculator prints them together.

How the per-hour figures are worked out

No practice tracks chair hours by carrier, and a tool demanding them could not be filled in from any report that exists. So hours are allocated between plans in proportion to gross production at your own fee schedule — your fee schedule is, by construction, your own pricing of chair time, so an hour billed at $600 of your fees is an hour of chair whatever a carrier later allows.

That assumption is worth stating plainly because everything per-hour rests on it, and it collapses to something simple: a plan's dollars per chair hour is just its reimbursement rate multiplied by what the practice produces per hour at its own fees. If your case mix under one carrier is unusually heavy or unusually quick relative to the rest of the practice, that plan's per-hour figure will be correspondingly off, and the reimbursement rate beside it — which needs no allocation at all — is the figure to trust.

What you need to fill it in

One production-by-carrier report for one month, your clinical chair hours, provider compensation and overhead for the same month. No patient-level information is needed or wanted: every input is a period total, which is what the report already gives you.

Common questions

What is an effective reimbursement rate?

Net production divided by gross production, for one carrier, over one period. If you billed $62,000 at your own fee schedule and wrote off $24,800 as a contractual adjustment, that plan reimbursed you at 60%. It is the only form in which two plans can be compared, and a practice management system reports the adjustment as a dollar column beside production rather than as a rate.

Why rank plans by write-off dollars instead of by reimbursement rate?

Because the worst rate is often not the biggest problem. A plan reimbursing 55% on $31,000 of production takes less out of the practice than one reimbursing 60% on $62,000. Ranking by rate points at the first; ranking by dollars points at the second. This page ranks by dollars and prints the rate beside it, so both readings are available and neither is hidden.

How can a plan pay less than an hour of chair time costs?

Your break-even reimbursement rate is what the chair costs to keep open divided by what you produce per hour at your own fees. Any plan reimbursing below that rate is buying chair time for less than the chair costs. This page states the break-even as a rate rather than as dollars so it lines up directly with the per-plan rates above it and the comparison is made by eye.

Why does raising my fee schedule not increase collections?

Because a PPO allowed fee is a contracted dollar amount, not a percentage of whatever the office charges. Raising your fees raises the gross production you bill and raises the contractual write-off by exactly the same amount on every contracted procedure. It collects more only on production that is not contracted. A practice where 80% of production runs through plans collects 20 cents of each added dollar and writes off the other 80.

How does the calculator work out chair hours per plan?

It allocates them in proportion to gross production at your own fee schedule, because no practice tracks chair hours by carrier and a tool that demanded them could not be filled in from any report that exists. Your fee schedule is your own pricing of chair time, so an hour billed at $600 of your fees is an hour of chair whatever a carrier later allows. The assumption is stated rather than hidden, and everything downstream follows from it.

Does dropping a plan recover the write-off?

No, and this page does not suggest it. Terminating a participating-provider agreement removes the write-off and the production together; whether the practice is better off depends on how much of that schedule refills at your own fees, which is a question about your market and your patients that no calculator can answer. The figures here say what each contract costs. What to do about a contract is a decision for you and your advisors.

Do I enter any patient information?

No. Every input is a period total for a carrier — production, write-off, chair hours, payroll, overhead — which is what a production-by-carrier report already gives you and which contains no protected health information. There is deliberately no shareable link and no upload: the calculator runs entirely in your browser, and saving a scenario writes the figures to this browser's own storage only.

Is this accounting, legal or contract advice?

No. It is your own numbers, divided. It makes no determination about how an adjustment should be recorded, about the terms of any participating-provider agreement, about tax treatment, or about whether to join or leave a network. Check every figure against your practice management system and your accounts, and against a qualified professional, before acting on it.

Work out your own rates

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, employment or contract advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, which networks to join or leave, how to code or record any adjustment, or how any agreement should be read. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every figure against your own practice management system, payroll records and accounts, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or acting on a contract with it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Carrier names above are used only to describe what the tool computes. No affiliation with, endorsement by, or sponsorship from any named company is implied.

which-ppo-contract-to-renegotiate-first..text:
DENTAL PRACTICE ECONOMICS

Which PPO contract should I renegotiate first?

Not the plan with the worst rate, and not a plan you happened to see nothing from this month. The calculator's own plan table already ranks every contract by write-off dollars and flags which ones sit below what the chair costs to run — this page walks through how to read those two things together before you pick up the phone.

Open the free calculator

Rank by dollars, not by rate

The contract worth a conversation first is the one taking the most money out of the practice, and that is very often not the one with the worst percentage. A plan reimbursing 55% on $31,000 of production writes off $13,950. A plan reimbursing 60% on $62,000 writes off $24,800 — nearly twice as much, on the better rate. A practice that renegotiates by rate alone spends its one conversation this quarter on the smaller number.

Delta PPO — 60% of $62,000
$24,800 write-off
Cigna — 55% of $31,000
$13,950 write-off

An illustration, not a benchmark or a survey of what any named carrier pays. Enter your own plans in the calculator to see your own ranking.

A zero-production plan is not evidence about its rate

The calculator's below-break-even flag deliberately skips any plan with no production for the period. A carrier you saw no patients from this month contributed no write-off either, so there is nothing in that row to judge — it is an absence, not a bad rate. Rating it anyway would put a contract on the "renegotiate this" list on the strength of a coincidence: the month you happened to check was slow for that plan, not the plan being underpriced. Look at a period where the plan actually saw production before deciding it belongs on the list.

Below break-even means the contract is worth a conversation, not a cancellation

A plan reimbursing below your break-even rate is buying chair time for less than the chair costs to keep open — that is a fact about the contract, stated as a rate so it lines up against the others by eye. It is not, on its own, a reason to drop the plan. Terminating a participating-provider agreement removes the write-off and the production together, and whether the practice comes out ahead depends on how much of that schedule refills at your own fees in your market — a question this page cannot answer for you. Renegotiating keeps the patients and asks for a better rate on them; that is the cheaper move to try first.

Renegotiating the schedule is not the same lever as raising your own fees

These get confused because both are described as "raising fees," and they collect in opposite ways. Your own posted fee schedule is what you charge; a PPO allowed fee is a dollar amount the contract fixes, and it does not move when your posted fee does. Raising your own fees raises what you bill on a contracted procedure and raises the write-off by exactly the same amount, so it collects almost nothing where a plan is heavily used. Renegotiating asks the carrier itself to raise the allowed fee — the only one of the two that actually changes what a PPO plan pays. If the goal is more cash from a specific contract, the conversation is with that carrier, not with your own fee schedule.

How many contracts is the write-off actually spread across?

The calculator's concentration reading counts carriers from the top of the ranked table until the running total reaches half the write-off. One or two contracts making up half of it is a concentrated practice: a focused push on those specific plans moves the whole number. Six or eight carriers splitting it close to evenly is a different situation — no single renegotiation moves much, and the more useful lever is often which plans a new patient is steered toward, not reworking an existing contract.

Before the call

Pull the ranked write-off table and the break-even line for a normal, representative month — not your slowest one and not your busiest. Note which contracts are both high on the write-off ranking and below break-even; that pair is the strongest case, because it says the contract is both expensive in dollars and unprofitable per chair hour. Bring the production and write-off figures the carrier's own claims already support — this page and the calculator only order your numbers, they do not draft the request or predict what any carrier will agree to.

Common questions

Which PPO contract should I renegotiate first?

The one taking the most write-off dollars, not the one with the worst rate — they are usually different contracts. A plan reimbursing 55% on $31,000 of production costs less than one reimbursing 60% on $62,000. Start the conversation with the carrier at the top of the calculator's plan table, ranked by dollars, and use the rate beside it to say by how much.

A plan shows zero production this month — is it the worst contract?

Not from this reading. A plan with no production this period contributed no write-off either, so it cannot be ranked against the others on a month where you saw nothing from it. The calculator excludes zero-production plans from its below-break-even flag for exactly this reason: rating a plan you did not use would send you to renegotiate a contract on the strength of a coincidence, not a rate. Check a period where the plan actually saw patients before judging it.

Does a plan below break-even mean I should drop it?

It means that plan is buying chair time for less than the chair costs to keep open — a fact about the contract, not a recommendation. Terminating a participating-provider agreement removes the write-off and the production together, and whether the practice is better off depends on how much of that schedule refills at your own fees. Renegotiating keeps the production and asks for a better rate on it; dropping trades the production away. Try the first before the second.

Is renegotiating a fee schedule the same as raising my own fees?

No, and the two collect very differently. Raising your own posted fee schedule raises what you bill and raises the contractual write-off by the same amount on every contracted procedure, so it collects almost nothing where a plan is heavily used. Renegotiating asks the carrier to raise the allowed fee itself — the contracted dollar amount your posted fee cannot move — which is the only lever of the two that changes what a PPO plan actually pays.

How many carriers make up half of my write-off?

The calculator counts it directly: starting from the biggest contract and adding the next until the running total reaches half the total write-off. One or two carriers taking half the write-off is a concentrated practice, worth a focused renegotiation push on those contracts. Eight carriers splitting it evenly is a different problem — no single conversation moves the total much, and the more useful lever is likely the plan mix a new patient is steered into, not any one existing contract.

Is this legal, contract or negotiation advice?

No. It ranks your own numbers and states which contract they say is worth a conversation; it does not tell you what to ask for, how to conduct the negotiation, or how any participating-provider agreement should be read or amended. Verify every figure against your practice management system and your accounts, and take the contract itself to a qualified professional before acting on it.
